title: Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy

paragraphs.en: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is an extracorporeal support technique that mimics renal function, primarily used for treating severe acute kidney injury (AKI), especially for patients with hemodynamic instability [1]. Through continuous blood purification employing various techniques with distinct solute clearance modalities, CRRT can effectively maintain patients’ internal homeostasis and reduce the burden on the kidneys. With the continuous development of technology, the application of CRRT has been expanded to support multiple organs, including cardiac, hepatic, and pulmonary functions, and can provide vital life support for patients with multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) [2]. However, CRRT is not a fixed intervention. Treatment initiation, modality selection, delivered dose, anticoagulation, net ultrafiltration, electrolyte management, filter performance, and liberation from therapy require repeated reassessment as the patient’s condition changes. This complexity poses substantial challenges to individualized treatment, efficient use of clinical resources, and consistent delivery of high-quality CRRT.

CRRT still faces several unresolved challenges in clinical practice. CRRT data come from multiple sources, such as electronic health records (EHRs), bedside monitors, laboratory systems, nursing records, and CRRT devices, and are often collected at different times and in different formats. Clinicians therefore need to interpret large amounts of heterogeneous and time-dependent information while managing common complications, including hemodynamic instability, circuit clotting or filter failure, electrolyte disturbances, and unplanned treatment interruptions [3–5]. CRRT initiation, treatment adjustment, and discontinuation remain difficult because patient characteristics and treatment responses vary across different patient groups and clinical settings. In addition, frequent alarms, limited clinical resources, and unequal access to nephrology expertise may further affect the consistency and quality of CRRT care.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges by analyzing complex clinical data, tracking changes over time, and predicting individual patient risks. Machine learning (ML) models have been developed to predict CRRT requirement, treatment-related hypotension, circuit clotting, successful discontinuation, renal recovery, and patient outcomes [6–11]. Large language models (LLMs) have also been explored for CRRT alarm management and patient education [12,13]. Currently, most AI studies in CRRT are retrospective or single-center, with relatively few models evaluated in independent cohorts or prospective clinical settings. The clinical relevance of these findings also varies across patient populations and settings, and some proposed applications have not yet been validated specifically in CRRT.

In this article, we review the current evidence and potential applications of AI in CRRT and discuss the challenges and strategies for its clinical implementation, aiming to support the development of AI-assisted CRRT management.

This narrative review was informed by a structured literature search to summarize the current evidence and potential applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). From inception to July 22, 2026, we searched three electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, and Scopus. The search strategy included two main concepts: CRRT-related terms and AI-related terms. The former included “continuous renal replacement therapy,” “continuous kidney replacement therapy,” “CKRT,” “CRRT,” “CVVH,” “CVVHD,” and “CVVHDF.” The latter included “algorithm,” “artificial intelligence,” “chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “clinical decision support,” “data-driven,” “deep learning,” “foundation model,” “generative AI,” “generative artificial intelligence,” “gradient boost,” “language model,” “large language model,” “long short-term memory,” “LSTM,” “machine learning,” “natural language processing,” “neural network,” “predictive model,” “random forest,” “reinforcement learning,” “support vector machine,” “transfer learning,” and “XGBoost.” Preprints, grey literature, and conference abstracts or reports lacking sufficient methodological details were excluded according to predefined eligibility criteria.

We also screened the reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews for additional relevant studies. After duplicate removal, two authors (X.L. and L.Z.) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved records to identify studies relevant to this review. Studies were eligible if they evaluated AI, machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, or other computational decision-support approaches in CRRT- or CKRT-related populations or clinical workflows. The two authors resolved disagreements through discussion and consensus. The study selection process is shown in Figure 1.

sections.title: AI framework and task-method matching in CRRT

paragraphs.en: Artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses a broad range of computational approaches. Machine learning (ML) is a major subset of AI, while deep learning (DL) is a subset of ML [14,15]. A comprehensive glossary of essential artificial intelligence (AI) terminology used in this manuscript is presented in Table 1. To facilitate interpretation of the models discussed in this review, simplified architectures of three representative approaches used in CRRT-related studies are illustrated in Figure 2.

Machine learning encompasses several learning paradigms, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning [16]. Among these, supervised learning uses labeled input-output pairs to learn a predictive mapping from input features to target outcomes [17,18], holding significant potential especially for clinical data [19], such as laboratory tests, vital signs, and medications. The clinical data are usually recorded in predetermined formats and fields, with values commonly represented as numerical measurements or discrete categorical entries. In CRRT research, supervised prediction models have been developed in specific patient populations to predict CRRT requirement, survival or mortality, hypotension, circuit clotting, successful discontinuation, and renal function recovery [7,8,10,11,20–22].

Deep learning typically uses multilayer neural networks and has shown increasing promise in medicine [23]. It can directly learn predictive representations and feature interactions from minimally curated data, thereby reducing reliance on manual variable selection and feature engineering [24]. Deep learning has been applied to EHR analysis, with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and related architectures processing complete, temporally ordered EHR data, including clinical notes where available, to predict in-hospital mortality, 30-day unplanned readmission, and prolonged length of stay [25]. Different deep-learning architectures can be selected according to the modality and structure of clinical data. Convolutional neural networks learn local features from neighboring pixels and aggregate them into global features, making them well suited to medical image classification [26]. RNNs are used for sequential data, while gated architectures such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent units control information flow over time and facilitate the learning of long-range dependencies [27–29]. In CRRT research, LSTM-based models have been used to predict the timing of CRRT initiation from daily clinical data, mortality from longitudinal fluid-balance and body-composition-monitoring data, and future transmembrane pressure (TMP) trajectories from data recorded by CRRT machines. In the mortality-prediction model, LSTM was used to process time-series data, whereas an autoencoder was incorporated to compensate for missing data [30–32].

Chatbots such as ChatGPT can support question answering and information provision. In CRRT, ChatGPT has been evaluated for patient-education questions and machine-alarm troubleshooting, primarily in terms of response accuracy, with consistency additionally assessed for alarm queries, rather than clinical outcomes [12,13]. Reinforcement learning (RL) is especially suited to sequential decision-making tailored to patients’ evolving characteristics. It has been used to develop dynamic renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation strategies and hierarchical clinical decision support for initiation and weaning timing, modality selection, and dynamic adjustment of ultrafiltration. However, prospective clinical testing is still required [33,34].

sections.title: AI in CRRT: Current and potential applications

paragraphs.en: In this section, we review the current evidence and potential applications of AI in CRRT (Figure 3). However, there are substantial differences in evidence maturity across application areas, and much of the current literature remains at the stage of retrospective model development, technical evaluation, or preliminary feasibility testing.

In CRRT management, AI and related computational approaches can facilitate the organization and analysis of complex clinical data, providing a basis for predictive modeling and clinical decision support. Ning and Zhang developed a deep learning framework combining the RoBERTa model and a bidirectional long short-term memory-conditional random field (BiLSTM-CRF) module to identify CRRT-indication entities from unstructured electronic medical records [35]. The framework achieved an F1 score of 92.9% when evaluated using retrospectively collected records from 568 adults receiving CRRT, but the study did not report independent external validation.

AI-based data processing can also provide inputs for downstream prediction. Using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) EHR dataset, Roy et al. applied deep neural networks to predict six intensive care unit (ICU) endpoints, including CRRT onset [36]. The study showed that multitask learning could support prediction when labeled data were limited, although it was based on a single EHR dataset. Its performance in other datasets and prospective settings remains to be established.

AI-based prediction models have been investigated for several CRRT-related tasks, including treatment timing, complication prediction, and prognostic assessment. In selected CRRT prediction tasks, machine-learning models showed higher discrimination than conventional clinical scoring systems [7,37]. Model performance should be interpreted in the context of the target population, outcome, predictors, and validation strategy [38,39], as most evidence remains retrospective with limited prospective validation.

The optimal timing of CRRT initiation remains uncertain, and available evidence suggests that the balance between earlier and delayed initiation may vary according to clinical context and patient characteristics [40–43]. Roy’s team used the MIMIC-III EHR dataset to train deep neural network models to predict the onset of six ICU endpoints, including CRRT. Compared with a single-task (ST) model, sequential subnetwork routing (SeqSNR) showed superior label efficiency. When the training labels for CRRT as the index task were reduced to 10%, SeqSNR achieved an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 44.2% and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 96.9%, compared with 42.5% and 96.7%, respectively, for the ST model [36]. The study was based on a single EHR dataset and predicted CRRT onset rather than the optimal timing of CRRT initiation.

For individualized RRT initiation, Grolleau et al. employed a doubly robust estimator with weighted least squares (dWOLS) within a reinforcement-learning framework to develop an interpretable dynamic decision-support system using MIMIC-III data. The primary outcome was hospital-free days at day 60 (HFD60) [33], and external validation was performed using data from the multicenter AKIKI and AKIKI2 trials. With the standard-delayed RRT initiation strategy as the reference, the crude and stringent strategies yielded estimated mean increases of 13.7 days (95% CI, −5.3 to 35.7) and 14.9 days (95% CI, −3.2 to 39.2) in HFD60, respectively. Neither effect estimate reached conventional statistical significance. Moreover, the study addressed RRT rather than CRRT specifically, and prospective testing remains necessary before broad clinical deployment.

At the other end of treatment, it is difficult to balance the risks of premature withdrawal against those of unnecessary continuation. In one study, nine machine-learning models were trained using MIMIC-IV data and externally validated in an independent hospital cohort, and XGBoost showed the highest external AUROC of 0.798 [9]. Another MIMIC-IV study used XGBoost to construct dynamic discontinuation models across four time points in 1,234 patients, achieving an AUC of 0.848 [44]. A separate retrospective analysis compared five algorithms for predicting successful CRRT discontinuation [22]. Among models based on five selected predictors, k-nearest neighbors (KNN) achieved the highest AUC of 0.870, whereas RF performed best when all available variables were included (AUC 0.875). These within-study shifts in model ranking suggest that algorithm performance may be sensitive to predictor selection. Nevertheless, differences in outcome definitions and validation strategies across studies limit direct comparison of model performance and highlight the need for further external and prospective validation before broader clinical application.

Prognostic applications of machine learning in CRRT have focused on short-term survival, mortality, and renal outcomes. Zamanzadeh et al. used EHR data from patients treated with CRRT at multiple institutions to train a model that predicted short-term survival after CRRT initiation. The model trained on the UCLA CRRT cohort achieved an AUROC of 0.835 internally; its AUROC decreased to 0.633 when evaluated in the Cedars-Sinai cohort. Models trained on multiple cohorts showed better cross-site generalization [11].

Other studies have examined mortality prediction using different machine-learning and validation strategies. LightGBM achieved the highest AUROC in the training cohort (0.954); by contrast, Lasso-regularized logistic regression performed best in the independent external cohort (AUROC 0.756) [45]. This change in model ranking indicates that superior performance during model development may not be maintained in an external population. In patients with sepsis-associated AKI receiving CRRT, eight machine-learning algorithms were evaluated using MIMIC-IV and eICU data, with external validation in an independent Chinese hospital cohort. Gradient boosting machine (GBM) achieved an AUC of 0.890 in the training cohort, which decreased to 0.756 in internal validation and 0.752 in external validation [46]. In a single-center retrospective cohort of 1,571 adults with AKI receiving CRRT, RF achieved the highest AUC for ICU mortality (0.784). This was higher than the AUCs of the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score (0.611), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score (0.677), and Mortality Scoring System for AKI with CRRT (MOSAIC) (0.722) [37]. The study used an internal 70:30 train-test split and did not include external validation. A separate cross-database analysis used 1,144 patients for model development and 391 for validation. In the validation cohort, RF achieved AUROCs of 0.80 and 0.78 for 10- and 90-day mortality, respectively [21].

Evidence has also extended beyond mortality to renal function recovery after CRRT. An externally validated Lasso-regularized logistic regression (Lasso-LR) model achieved an AUROC of 0.748 [10], although the authors noted suboptimal calibration and relatively low Kappa values, particularly in the external cohort. Longer-term kidney outcomes have also been examined. A CoxBoost model for predicting progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) after CKRT was developed using data from six hospitals and externally validated in two hospitals. It achieved C-indices of 0.811 and 0.742 in internal and external validation, respectively [47]. These studies highlight the importance of external validation, calibration, and evaluation across different patient populations and clinical settings rather than relying on internal discrimination alone. Differences in patient characteristics, disease severity, treatment practices, and data sources may influence the distribution of predictors and the relationship between predictors and outcomes. Different outcome definitions also imply different clinical prediction tasks with varying levels of difficulty. Therefore, AUC/AUROC values should be interpreted within the context of study design and validation setting rather than used to directly rank different algorithms. Selected model comparisons emphasizing external validation, transportability, and model-ranking changes are summarized in Table 2.

sections.title: Real-time monitoring and dynamic parameter prediction

paragraphs.en: Real-time CRRT data provide a basis for time-series prediction of changing treatment parameters. Using more than 20,000 min of data from 405 CRRT cases, an LSTM-based framework estimated transmembrane pressure trajectories over a 50-min horizon. In simulated treatment evaluations, the model achieved recall rates >0.97 and F2 scores >0.93 and provided an average warning approximately 23 min before TMP reached the predefined 260-mmHg threshold associated with substantial filter clotting [32]. These findings support the feasibility of using time-series machine data for earlier recognition of circuit deterioration. Prospective evaluation is still needed to determine whether model-guided warnings improve circuit lifespan or clinical management.

Machine-learning methods have been explored for predicting CRRT-related complications and supporting anticoagulation management. Current evidence mainly involves hemodynamic instability, circuit clotting, and regional citrate anticoagulation.

In 2,349 adults with AKI, Kang et al. developed models to predict a ≥ 20-mmHg reduction in mean arterial pressure within 6 h after CRRT initiation. XGBoost achieved the highest AUROC of 0.828, followed by a deep neural network (0.822) and LightGBM (0.813), with higher discrimination than conventional disease-severity scores [7]. More recently, Qiu et al. evaluated six machine-learning algorithms in 1,103 patients with ESKD receiving CRRT. SVM achieved an AUC of 0.773 for predicting a ≥ 20-mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure within 6 h and showed similar performance in temporal validation (AUC 0.778) [49]. Although SVM performed consistently across different definitions of intradialytic hypotension, the retrospective single-center design and lack of independent external validation limit assessment of cross-center generalizability. A pediatric study evaluated machine-learning models for intradialytic hypotension using clinical and dialysis-machine pressure data from 38 CKRT admissions in 23 children, with CatBoost showing the best overall performance. The Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations method identified dialysis-machine-derived time-series pressure variables as important predictors [50].

In 212 patients receiving anticoagulant-free CRRT, ensemble learning achieved an AUC of 0.863 for predicting circuit coagulation within 24 h, whereas random forest was the best individual model, with an AUC of 0.819. The ensemble combined random forest and XGBoost using a soft voting strategy that incorporates the confidence of individual classifiers. The investigators also noted that this approach may retain good generalization when data are limited. Platelet count, filtration fraction, and triglycerides were the three most important predictors [8].

In a separate cohort of 636 patients with ESKD undergoing CRRT, SVM achieved the highest AUC of 0.864, compared with 0.815 for XGBoost and 0.717 for logistic regression. SVM also showed better calibration and greater net benefit across most decision thresholds. The authors attributed this advantage to its ability to capture nonlinear interactions in complex clinical data [51]. SHAP analysis identified the initial low-molecular-weight heparin dose, platelet count, and ultrafiltration quantity as the three most important features. The study proposed prospective multicenter validation, improved data preprocessing, and incorporation of dynamic data to enable prediction in real time. A pediatric CKRT study developed a machine-learning model from time-series treatment data collected across 88 evaluable sessions involving 23 patients to predict clotting events 60 min in advance. Effluent volume, treatment duration, fluid removal, and dialysate flow were among the important predictors [52]. Although the study included more than 218,000 time-series data points, the number of individual patients was small, and independent external validation was not performed.

Across these studies, most models were developed retrospectively in single-center cohorts and lacked independent external validation. Differences in patient populations, anticoagulation strategies, outcome definitions, and the use of static versus time-series predictors also limit direct comparison between models. Prospective multicenter evaluation is needed before these tools can be used to guide complication management. Representative machine-learning studies of CRRT/CKRT-related hypotension and circuit clotting are summarized in Table 3.

Available CRRT studies applying machine learning to anticoagulation have examined regional citrate anticoagulation. Chen et al. compared AdaBoost, XGBoost, SVM, and a shallow neural network for predicting post-filter ionized calcium categories. The model also provided recommendations for adjusting citrate and 10% calcium gluconate infusion at the point of care [53]. The shallow neural network showed the best overall classification performance among the evaluated algorithms. The authors related this advantage to its ability to learn complex relationships between input and output variables. The model was subsequently evaluated using data from Peking Union Medical College Hospital and the MIMIC-III database. However, differences in clinical settings and post-filter ionized calcium ranges limited direct comparison between the two databases. Prospective multicenter validation in larger cohorts is needed to assess prediction performance and generalizability across clinical settings.

More recently, Mali et al. evaluated an edge-computing and federated-learning framework for citrate-overdose detection and anticoagulation adjustment using MIMIC-IV data [54]. Accuracy reached 0.962 under independent and identically distributed (IID) conditions and 0.957 under non-IID conditions. Prospective studies have not yet established whether these approaches reduce anticoagulation-related complications or improve patient outcomes.

AI may support individualized CRRT management by integrating diverse information, such as clinical data, treatment information, and pharmacokinetic data, into clinical decision support systems. Li et al. developed machine learning models using data from 48,000 virtual patients across 24 simulated dosing scenarios and externally validated them in 78 critically ill CRRT patients [55]. The models predicted two pharmacodynamic targets: maintaining free meropenem concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) throughout the dosing interval (100% fT > MIC), or above four times the MIC (100% fT > 4 × MIC). In external validation, RF and XGBoost achieved the highest AUCs for 100% fT > MIC (0.919 each), whereas gradient boosting (GB) performed best for 100% fT > 4 × MIC (AUC 0.929). GB was selected for the decision support system because of its balanced performance across both targets. Direct prediction of pharmacodynamic target attainment, rather than intermediate pharmacokinetic estimates, may partly explain its advantage over conventional population pharmacokinetic modeling. SHAP analysis identified MIC, dosing interval, dose amount, infusion rate, CRRT clearance, and creatinine clearance as key predictors. The model was incorporated into the MeroDose web application. Despite external validation, the model was developed largely from simulated data, leaving its clinical benefit in routine CRRT practice uncertain.

Multicenter collaboration can broaden the data used to develop AI models for CRRT and provide independent settings for their evaluation. Zamanzadeh et al. developed a CRRT survival model using EHR data from multiple institutions and found that models trained on data from multiple cohorts showed better generalization than models trained on a single cohort [11]. In a multicenter retrospective study, Yoo et al. analyzed 784 patients with severe AKI requiring CRRT from eight tertiary hospitals in Korea. Their deep-learning model incorporated repeated fluid-balance measurements and predicted mortality better than classical machine-learning methods, supporting the use of fluid-balance monitoring for prognosis assessment during CRRT [31]. The CRRT-weaning models developed in the Rouen cohort were subsequently tested in two independent cohorts, one from Rennes and the other derived from MIMIC-IV. This dual validation allowed the models to be assessed in two different clinical contexts [48].

AI may support healthcare professionals by assisting with CRRT troubleshooting and clinical decision-making. Sheikh et al. evaluated ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 using 50 CRRT machine alarm questions selected and verified by critical care nephrologists [12]. In two testing rounds, ChatGPT 4 correctly answered 90% and 94% of the questions, with 92% agreement between rounds (κ = 0.88). Although its accuracy and consistency were numerically higher than those of ChatGPT 3.5, the differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, the evaluation relied on predetermined answer keys in a controlled setting rather than real clinical decisions. The remaining errors are particularly relevant for CRRT, where inappropriate responses to machine alarms may compromise treatment safety. A practical role for LLMs may therefore be to assist with basic device alerts while maintaining clinician oversight and using training data that cover diverse clinical scenarios and terminology. Available studies of LLMs in CRRT have primarily focused on predefined question-answering tasks, including CRRT alarm troubleshooting and patient education scenarios, while real-world evaluations within clinical workflows remain limited. Future studies should evaluate LLM-based tools in clinical settings and assess whether they improve CRRT-related workflows and support safe decision-making. Candidate outcomes may include response accuracy, time required for problem resolution, clinician workload, user acceptance, and safety events.

The design of decision support systems also needs to reflect clinicians’ working practices. In a predevelopment survey of 171 ICU physicians, 66.1% considered an AI-based clinical decision support system useful for CRRT weaning, and 95.3% considered it important to understand the criteria underlying its predictions [56]. Most physicians preferred predictions at a specific time, such as morning rounds, and favored integration into existing ICU software rather than a separate interface. These findings suggest that useful CRRT decision support should fit existing workflows, provide interpretable predictions with an indication of certainty, and avoid unnecessary continuous alerts.

Current CRRT-specific evidence for AI in patient communication and education is largely limited to information provision. Sheikh et al. evaluated ChatGPT 4 using 89 patient education questions from the Mayo Clinic Handbook, including 50 related to CRRT and 39 to AKI [13]. For CRRT questions, appropriate responses were obtained for 96% of the original and adverb-altered questions and 98% of those containing incomplete sentences or misspellings, with no significant differences across formats. This robustness may be useful in clinical communication, where patients and families may use incomplete expressions, misspell unfamiliar medical terms, or have different levels of health literacy. The study nevertheless used predefined questions rather than interactions with actual patients, so accuracy alone does not establish effective patient education.

Further development could focus on adapting educational content to lower literacy levels, assessing retention of key information, and using prompt engineering or model fine-tuning to improve the empathy and engagement of responses. Beyond information provision, chatbots have also been discussed as potential communication tools in critical care nephrology, including in sensitive clinical contexts [57]. Although AI-based patient education and chatbot interventions have shown potential to reduce anxiety and improve treatment adherence in other clinical settings [58–60], evidence for these patient-centered outcomes in CRRT remains lacking. Representative studies across the main applications of AI in CRRT are summarized in Table 4.

sections.title: Data quality, standardization, and model transportability

paragraphs.en: Retrospective CRRT AI studies are often based on relatively small cohorts and internal validation, which may increase the risk of overfitting and optimistic performance estimates and limit reproducibility [8,37,52]. External validation has also revealed limited model transportability; for example, Zamanzadeh et al. reported a decrease in AUROC from 0.835 internally to 0.633 at an external center [11]. Prospective multicenter validation is therefore needed before routine clinical implementation [48,51].

Standardization should therefore address data structure and terminology, as well as the definition, measurement, and preprocessing of predictors and outcomes. The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) common data model has supported structural and semantic harmonization across CRRT cohorts, while Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) may facilitate real-time interoperability [48]. In addition to data standardization, practical deployment of AI in CRRT may be limited by differences in hardware interfaces, data accessibility, hospital information technology (IT) infrastructure, and the need for middleware solutions to connect device-generated data with clinical information systems. Future implementation will require collaboration among device manufacturers, healthcare institutions, and information technology teams to establish interoperable and secure data pathways.

When cross-center differences persist, site-specific dynamic models and subgroup evaluation may help identify variations in performance [11]. Future AI-CRRT studies should prespecify validation strategies, distinguish training, tuning, and evaluation datasets, and report model performance and prespecified CRRT-related clinical outcomes. The TRIPOD+AI statement, an update of the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) guideline, guides clear and complete reporting of prediction-model studies [38]. PROBAST+AI, an update of the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST), supports assessment of model quality, risk of bias, and applicability [39]. The Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials-Artificial Intelligence (SPIRIT-AI) and Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials-Artificial Intelligence (CONSORT-AI) extensions provide reporting guidance for AI clinical trial protocols and reports [61,62].

For AI to be useful in CRRT, clinicians need to understand its outputs and use them within routine clinical workflows. ICU physicians preferred AI-based decision support to be integrated into existing clinical software, with predictions provided at specific clinical time points rather than continuously. Most physicians also considered it important to understand the factors behind model predictions [56]. AI should support rather than replace clinical judgment [63].

Device interoperability is another practical barrier to AI implementation in CRRT. Older or non-connected CRRT platforms may have limited standardized data-export capabilities and may require additional interfaces or middleware to integrate machine data with EHRs and AI-based monitoring systems [40,64]. Although CRRT connectivity platforms have demonstrated the feasibility of automated machine-data transfer, upgrading heterogeneous equipment may require additional information technology infrastructure and technical maintenance, while CRRT-specific evidence on retrofit costs remains limited [64].

This is also important for large language models. ChatGPT showed high accuracy on predefined questions about CRRT alarms and patient education [12,13]. These studies evaluated answer accuracy rather than bedside clinical decisions or patient outcomes. LLMs may generate hallucinated or otherwise incorrect information, and their responses may vary with prompt wording and the information provided. The use of identifiable patient information in external systems may also create privacy risks. LLM outputs should therefore be verified by clinicians before they are used to inform clinical decisions [63,65]. Similarly, explainable AI methods such as SHAP can help identify how individual variables contribute to model predictions [48], but these factors should be interpreted together with patient characteristics, laboratory findings, and CRRT-related parameters. For example, when a CRRT model predicts a high risk of mortality or treatment failure, features identified by SHAP should be interpreted as factors associated with the prediction rather than direct causes of the outcome.

Good model performance alone is not enough for clinical implementation. Before clinical use, model performance should be evaluated using data that were not used for model development and that represent the intended patient population [38,39]. Evaluation should include discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and performance in important patient subgroups [38,39]. Models with acceptable performance should then be evaluated prospectively to determine their safety, effects on clinical decisions, and effects on patient outcomes. Popoff et al. proposed a similar staged approach for their CRRT-weaning model, with prospective evaluation followed by randomized testing if the initial results were favorable [48].

Clinical implementation also requires attention to data security, patient privacy, bias, and responsibility for AI-assisted decisions [63]. Clinical AI is increasingly shaped by international and national frameworks, including guidance from the World Health Organization, China’s guidance for AI medical devices, the European Union AI Act, and Good Machine Learning Practice principles [66–69]. Nephrology-specific ethical guidance has also emerged [70], while a dedicated regulatory framework for AI in CRRT has not yet been established. Cost, staff training, and integration with existing clinical systems should also be considered [63]. Although some studies suggest that AI-supported anemia management may be cost-effective in hemodialysis patients [71,72], economic evidence specific to CRRT remains lacking. Model performance and fairness should continue to be assessed after implementation [39]. In CRRT, a practical approach would be to move from retrospective model development and evaluation in independent data to prospective clinical evaluation, followed by clinician-supervised use and continued assessment of clinical impact, cost, and model performance. Implementation should be adapted to institutional readiness, considering factors such as data availability, digital infrastructure, workflow integration, and capacity for AI model evaluation [73]. Centers with limited resources may begin with validated tools using routinely available clinical data, centers with moderate resources may add local prospective validation and workflow integration, and centers with advanced resources may progress to real-time device integration and locally adapted models.

The integration of AI into the ICU environment may raise important ethical, legal, and equity concerns. As an important organ-support therapy for critically ill patients, AI-assisted CRRT is also subject to these concerns as it moves toward clinical implementation. Critically ill patients may have impaired decision-making capacity because of acute illness, while time-sensitive clinical circumstances can limit opportunities for adequate communication [74]. The opacity of “black-box” AI systems may further complicate informed consent by making the basis of AI-assisted recommendations, their limitations, and associated risks more difficult to explain [75,76]. Liability for AI-associated harm remains incompletely defined and may involve clinicians, healthcare institutions, and AI developers, while the complexity and opacity of AI systems can make accountability more difficult [77]. Algorithmic fairness for vulnerable ICU populations also needs attention, as critical-care datasets may under-represent certain patient groups or lack sociodemographic information needed to detect subgroup disparities [78,79].

Future AI-assisted CRRT may make greater use of longitudinal data from electronic health records and CRRT machines [40]. The addition of bedside biochemical measurements could provide additional information for dynamic assessment. Ion-sensitive organic electrochemical transistors have already been evaluated for Na+, K+, and Ca2+ measurement in clinical CRRT effluent samples [80]. Combining these measurements with physiological, laboratory, and treatment data may allow AI models to track changes during CRRT more comprehensively and support more individualized clinical decisions.

Another future direction is more individualized treatment. An ML-based decision-support system for meropenem dosing combined patient, dosing, and CRRT-related variables and was externally evaluated using clinical CRRT data [55]. Prospective evaluation is still needed to determine whether such tools improve treatment decisions or patient outcomes. Online physiological and chemical sensors, together with miniaturized and wearable blood-purification devices, have been proposed for future CRRT development [81], but these concepts remain hypothetical and require clinical validation. Related hemodialysis literature has linked real-time monitoring and predictive models with the development of more personalized and miniaturized dialysis systems [82].

Future research should follow a staged pathway toward clinical translation. The initial priority is multicenter prospective validation with assessment of model performance, generalizability, clinical utility, and safety. Following validation, integration of AI tools with CRRT devices and clinical workflows should be explored to enable real-time decision support. Further refinement of explainable AI approaches and health-economic evaluation will be important to improve transparency, clinician acceptance, and sustainable implementation [83,84]. Economic evaluations should prioritize clinically relevant applications, including treatment optimization, complication prediction, and workflow management, and assess infrastructure costs, maintenance, labor burden, and potential reductions in complications and resource utilization.

The integration of AI with CRRT represents an emerging area of research in healthcare. While clinical implementation remains nascent, its potential applications, including optimizing CRRT workflows and supporting patient communication and education, have gradually expanded. To support the safe and effective implementation of AI in CRRT, challenges related to data quality, external validation, ethical considerations, and technical integration need to be systematically addressed. A pragmatic implementation pathway may progress from independent and prospective evaluation to integration into clinical workflows under clinician supervision. More advanced integration of device data may be considered where resources and infrastructure permit, with continued assessment of safety and performance. With continued technological development and clinical validation, AI-assisted CRRT may play an increasingly important role in supporting personalized treatment and improving clinical management.

tables.xml:
Glossary of key artificial intelligence terms.

AI terminologyConcise definition
Artificial intelligence (AI)A machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.
Machine learning (ML)The development and use of computer systems that adapt and learn from data with the goal of improving accuracy.
Supervised learningA type of machine learning in which a model learns to predict explicit labels or output values for data.
Reinforcement learning (RL)Learning what to do—how to map situations to actions—so as to maximize a numerical reward signal.
Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)A scalable tree boosting method that sequentially combines decision trees to improve predictive performance.
Random forest (RF)An ensemble learning method that combines multiple randomized decision trees and aggregates their predictions for classification or regression.
Support vector machine (SVM)A supervised learning method that identifies a decision boundary that maximizes separation between classes, with kernel functions allowing nonlinear relationships to be modeled.
Deep learning (DL)Computational models composed of multiple processing layers that learn representations of data with multiple levels of abstraction.
Feed-forward neural network (FNN)A neural network in which information flows from the input through one or more intermediate layers to the output without recurrent feedback connections.
Recurrent neural network (RNN)A type of neural network tailored to handle sequential data.
Long short-term memory (LSTM)A recurrent architecture that introduces gate functions into the cell structure to handle long-term dependencies.
Autoencoder (AE)A multilayer neural network that learns low-dimensional codes and reconstructs the input from those codes.
Natural language processing (NLP)A field that transforms human communication into forms suitable for computer use and analysis.
Large language model (LLM)AI tools specifically trained to process and generate text.
ChatbotA computer program designed to simulate human text or verbal conversations.
Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), including Shapley additive explanations (SHAP)Approaches intended to make learned models and decisions understandable to end users; SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction.
